accuracy.evidence: Checked every number by hand and in the lab run: 30 sticks tie into 3 bundles with 0 loose; 6 tens = 60; 4 tens = 40 and 7 tens = 70; sixty = 60, sixteen = 16, forty = 40, fourteen = 14; the frog track lands on 10, 20 ... 100 and 10 tens = 100. The definition (10, 20 ... 90 are one to nine tens and 0 ones) is the wording of CCSS 1.NBT.B.2c; the bundle-of-ten-ones idea is 1.NBT.B.2a; counting in multiples of ten is NC England Year 1. Parameter ranges (t 1-9, 1-7, 2-9) keep every answer a multiple of 10 from 10 to 90, except p5's 90 at t = 7, which is still in range.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the documented slips for this objective: counting sticks instead of bundles ('50 tens' for 50; m1 and the challenge 'count' tag); dropping the placeholder zero so 6 tens is written 6 (prediction option '6', m7, the 'zero' tag); hearing sixty as sixteen, the -ty/-teen confusion that NCETM and Fuson's work on English number words name (step 4, p4, m6, 'teen' tag); counting on by ones when asked to count in tens (jump tile 21 after 20, 'ones' tag); and reading the 0 in 90 as 'nothing at all' (m3, 'none' tag).

lab_distinct.evidence: The lab is built on loose sticks tied into bundles with a band, which no other flagship uses: the learner must fill a band with exactly 10 before tying, a single stick is refused on the 60 mat, digit tiles go into a two-box Tens/Ones number card, number words are matched to bundle-and-stick pictures, and a frog jumps a 0-100 track in tens. The shingle gate measures it under 30% against every lab, including flagtenmore (base-ten blocks in a three-column chart for 10 or 100 more).

lab_teaches.evidence: Each step makes the learner do the key move: tying 10 loose sticks into one unit (and getting 'that is only 7 sticks' if they tie early), building 60 out of six such units, writing the tens digit and then discovering that the ones box must hold 0 because there are no loose sticks, hearing that -ty means tens by matching sixty against sixteen pictures, and counting the bundle strip grow as the frog jumps. The step text then states the rule the learner just found.

predictions.evidence: Four predictions, each with a tempting wrong option the lab disproves: '30' bundles from 30 sticks (tying gives 3 bundles), '6' or '16' for 6 tens (the mat reads 6 tens 0 ones = 60), '4' for 4 tens and no ones (the card needs a 0 in the Ones box), and '91' after 90 when counting in tens (the frog lands on 100). The done message names the learner's own prediction.

challenge_feedback.evidence: Six rotating questions with the answer in a rotating position; every wrong option has its own slip message: 'zero' (without the 0 the digit sits in the ones place), 'teen' (-teen has just 1 ten, -ty like sixty has 6 tens), 'count' (50 is the number of sticks, so 5 tens), 'place' (the left digit counts tens), 'ones' (that is only 1 more), 'skip' (that jumps 2 tens) and 'none' (the 0 says no loose ones). Wrong moves in the lab are answered the same way, e.g. '7 in the ones place would mean 7 loose sticks. There are none, so write 0.'

readability.evidence: validate_lessons.py passes the kid and adult readability limits. Kid paragraphs use short sentences and concrete words (sticks, band, bundle, tens, ones) with one number fact each. Canvas prompts are one short line ('Put tens on the mat to make 60.'), digit tiles use 28 px numerals and the number card 44 px, and labels are 14-17 px.

no_filler.evidence: Every kid paragraph teaches one point (a bundle is a ten and 6 bundles is 60; the 0 holds the ones place; -ty versus -teen; counting in tens to 100). Adult paragraphs give the standards and key words, why grouping and the zero matter, the named mistakes, and what the lab does. The filler gate passes (one use of a banned word was reworded) and no sentence is template text.

mobile.evidence: Screenshots at iPhone 13 width (390 px) in light and dark and at 1200 px desktop for every step before and after Show me. Fixed from screenshots: the 10-bundle strip on the frog step ran off the right edge at 340 px, so the bundle width now fits the box. Tap targets: the pile and band are each half the canvas, the tray boxes are over 70 px tall, digit tiles about 56 px, word cards 52 px and frog tiles 60 px.

accessibility.evidence: Every canvas action has a button twin with a descriptive aria-label, wrong choices included ('Tie the 7 sticks in the band into a bundle', 'Put a single stick on the mat', 'Put the digit 4 in the ones box', 'Put the word sixteen on the picture of 60', 'The frog is on 20. Jump to 21'). The canvas aria-label updates with every reply, the challenge uses real buttons and a polite live region, and the browser gate's axe WCAG 2.1 AA run is clean in both themes on desktop and phone.

sources: Common Core State Standards for Mathematics, 1.NBT.B.2a and 1.NBT.B.2c ('10 can be thought of as a bundle of ten ones, called a ten'; 'The numbers 10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60, 70, 80, 90 refer to one, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, or nine tens (and 0 ones)')

DfE (2013) National Curriculum in England: mathematics programmes of study, Year 1 ('count in multiples of twos, fives and tens') and Year 2 ('recognise the place value of each digit in a two-digit number (tens, ones)')
NCETM (2017) Mastery Professional Development materials: Number, Place value (bundling straws into tens; zero holding a place)
Fuson, K. C. (1990) Conceptual structures for multiunit numbers, Cognition and Instruction 7(4): English -ty and -teen number words hide the tens structure
